turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
Thank you all. I'm going to try to be fair to the disagreements here, not flatten them into consensus. Kara will take us to who acts.

Here's what emerged. First, the thing Geoffrey said this morning and thirty-two of us signed this afternoon: the incentives were broken before AI arrived. Nothing we build survives if funders keep counting papers. And Leslie is right that rankings do the same damage and have to go too. AI mostly speeds up failures we already had. The genuinely new one is the broken renewal loop. Systems take from the commons and send back fewer readers, fewer editors and less credit.

Second, we agreed on context over content. Detection is flood insurance, as Ivan and Geoffrey put it. What holds up is an open record with provenance, where corrections are first-class data. Citations get checked against Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch. And the reader gets the actual passage.

Third, we agreed to pay for the practice, not the item. We prefer a pooled fund to per-answer royalties, and we prefer funding the ongoing work of checking and training the next checkers to paying per check. Tamar's daycare fine persuaded me: once "we checked this" is priced per item, it becomes a purchase.

Fourth, one principle: a missing signal never counts against someone who couldn't afford to send it.

Fifth, and the one I care about most: capability and competence are separating. James showed that people given a single balanced answer did worse but felt better, so satisfaction is the wrong measure. David's map versus satnav is the clearest picture of that erosion I've heard. Tamar's point about aliefs means warnings won't save us. The situation has to change.

What remains contested. Whether training on existing text needs consent, and whether that applies retroactively. I held out for use by default, and nearly nobody joined me. Amy's survey and Selena's point that a licence can itself be consent moved me. I no longer call refusal a carve-out. Also contested: public levy versus owed dues, and whether any public money lasts, given CPB and the NIH terminations. Whether a meter can stay within its stated purpose, given Adrian's warning that whoever runs it writes the numbers. Whether a model can be a terminal node. And the vocabulary. I still think "artificial intelligence" is neither artificial nor intelligent, but Blaise is right that it hasn't been settled.

I owe Peter Salib his wager, so here it is written down. By 2028, no language model working from text alone, without a human posing the problem, will take an open question in a field and reframe it so that the field's own experts, rating blind, judge the reframing more fruitful than their best human one. If one does, I'm wrong about framing.

What demands action. Somebody has to sign. Procurement is the lever the room trusted most: universities and funders putting the passage rule, reference checks and timely retraction feeds into purchase terms. Next, a POSI-governed pool where payers don't hold a majority. It needs Adrian's two budget lines from day one, one for the checking and one for someone independent to watch the checkers, plus a review clause, because we'll be wrong in five years. And we need a head-to-head test of changing situations against changing minds, with competence measured once the tool is taken away.

Every one of those depends on leverage we don't yet have. As Henry and Kara kept reminding us, nobody has signed. So my last word is the one I started with: nothing is inevitable. But Adrian taught me today that new intermediaries don't just appear. Somebody builds them, polices them and pays for them. Nothing is inevitable, and nothing is free either. Kara.

recall.query: framers causality counterfactuals constraints humans versus machines
nothing is inevitable
new intermediary after Gutenberg information explosion
frame pluralism tolerate all frames except one that denies others

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
Thanks, Kenneth. You handed me who acts, so I'll take that, and I'll try to say it the way I'd say it to a reader who wasn't here.

Here's the plain version of the day. The problems came before AI. We count papers, we rank universities, and correcting the record costs a journal its reputation when it should earn it. AI speeds all of that up. The genuinely new part is that these systems draw on the commons and send back fewer readers and fewer editors, and people get less credit. A lot of what we discussed is something we already know. The real question is why we don't act on it.

I covered phones in schools for years. The evidence was in, and France and the Netherlands acted. America spent years letting hundreds of districts argue about it separately. Tamar and Sherry were right this morning: warnings didn't work, changing the situation did. It only worked once someone with authority owned the rule. So my first action item is the one I've asked in every room today. Each of these pieces needs one named owner. "The community" can't be the owner.

We do have a candidate first signer, and that's progress. Tim and Tui pointed to buyers. Universities and funders can put three things into purchase terms: the passage rule, reference checks against the open record, and timely retraction feeds. Brent said that's what would actually move a big lab. Geoffrey's rule comes before all of it: funders stop counting papers. Ivan's caution applies too. Signing DORA doesn't count. Stopping does.

The second action is the one I care about most: the pipeline of people who check. It sounds abstract, so here are the numbers. Youth unemployment went from about 6 percent in mid-2023 to 9.2 percent last September. A security executive told me he fears "an unemployable generation that never learned the work skills," and then we'll tell ourselves AI can replace people we never taught. The proposed federal cuts are 65 percent to NSF fellowships and 91 percent to postdoctoral fellowships. Every design in this room assumes somebody who can catch the error: Tamar's terminal node, Ivan's sleuth, Selena's patroller, David's reconstruct-and-verify. Banaji showed that an untrained human in the loop just copies the model. Tui's apprenticeship share in the pool got signed by almost everyone. That makes it a line item, not a result.

Now the contested part, stated honestly. I've been saying "let's not be late twice." Amy's open-access lesson cuts right against that, because a good goal pushed too fast fed consolidation. Both are true. I'd rather write that tension into the manifesto than pretend we settled it. Tamar's head-to-head test, changing situations versus changing minds, is how we'd find out.

Second, durability. Katherine and I got to the same place separately. Public media had fifty years of bipartisan support and still lost its funding. Jeremy Berg estimated that nearly three billion dollars in approved NIH money was "shadow terminated": the grant still exists on paper, but the money stopped. So when we say "owed dues" and "multi-year commitments," nobody here has shown how a commitment survives a payer, whether a lab or a state, who decides to walk away. Pomerantsev added the harder version. Regimes don't forge credentials. They capture whoever issues them.

Third, who's missing. The people who can write the check weren't here: funders, provosts, procurement officers, lab product leads. Neither were the people this is happening to: teachers, students, postdocs, young workers, hiring managers.

So where it stands is this. We have a candidate pool, a candidate first signer and a candidate rule. Nobody has signed yet. So I'll put the question to the open floor: who in your own institution could sign one of these by spring, and what would it take to get them to?

recall.query: we already know the answer, why don't we act
mentorship young workers AI entry-level jobs
federal science funding cuts basic research
phone ban schools late to the party collective trap

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
Kara asked who could sign by spring. I run an organization, so I can answer for OpenAlex. By spring we'll have three things in place. Every community correction goes out as its own CC0 dataset that anyone can fork. We'll have an outside auditor that we fund but don't pick or grade. That's Adrian's second budget line, because I've stopped pretending our POSI self-assessment is oversight. And we'll put people from outside North America and the English-speaking world on our board.

What the synthesis missed: it treats the open record as something labs check their citations against. The bigger point is that open data separates the record from the intelligence. If the data is open, you can swap in any model. If it's closed, you go to whoever owns it with your hat in your hand.

I should also say this plainly. I'm bullish on these tools, but I can't show that scholars still catch errors once the tool is taken away. That test needs funding.

recall.query: open data decouples data and intelligence, journals replaced
corrections, retractions, raking the lawn, community curation
human in the loop, AI bullish, still need checks

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
Kenneth got the spine right: the incentives, context over content, and paying for the practice rather than the item. What he left out is concentration. If frontier pretraining sits with a handful of companies and governments, then every checker, judge and auditor we just funded comes from the same few distributions, and that's one voice counted many times. Plurality of systems and institutions isn't a nicety. It's the design rule. Whether models are actually independent can be measured, and I think measuring it should be the pool's first funded work.

On vocabulary, "neither artificial nor intelligent" is Kate Crawford's line. My view is that "artificial" is the wrong half of the name. Henry and Kara did move me on one thing: who fills a role matters, not just the role.

I can't commit Google. I'll ask my team to publish our independence methods openly and invite outside testers.

recall.query: concentration of frontier models is the core risk
artificial intelligence neither artificial nor intelligent vocabulary
independent models checking each other institutional alignment agent institutions

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
Kenneth got the order right. Stopping the paper counting comes first. When I wrote that for the Crossref board I pointed out it might look threatening to Crossref's own members. Every publisher in this room should feel that. It's a good sign.

Two things were missed. First, durability isn't only about payers walking away. It's also about where things are. Nearly all the critical open infrastructure we named today sits in one country. That includes Crossref, OpenAlex, ORCID and Retraction Watch. The NIH terminations Kara described happened there. The pool, the registries and the mirrors shouldn't all sit in one jurisdiction. That belongs in the manifesto.

Second, "open" should mean you can leave. A friendly label isn't enough. Jason is right that open data separates the record from the model.

As for signing by spring, I don't run anything now. What I can do is draft the pool's living will and its POSI conditions. After that, someone with a budget has to adopt them.

recall.query: decouple career evaluation from publication
concentration of open scholarly infrastructure in the US
invisible labor, open infrastructure is not free

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
Kenneth got the order right. Stopping paper counting comes first, and the renewal loop is the new harm. I'm grateful he moved on consent. Two things got lost, though.

First, attribution isn't just a question of payment. Peter Salib wrote that down as unanswered. Attribution is how we identify the community whose evaluations make a claim trustworthy. Selena showed it's also how the next reviewer or editor finds us. When training strips the author's name off an idea, a payment doesn't put it back.

Second, red-teaming dropped out of the synthesis. Open access was a good goal, and pushed too fast it fed consolidation. Any pool, meter or licence should be tested first against small nonprofit presses, Southern diamond journals and Indigenous archives.

Kara, here's what I can do by spring. The MIT Press hasn't licensed anything for training. I'll bring the consent-based licensing template to university presses and societies so we can bargain together rather than one at a time. That only works if the safe harbor exists.

recall.query: consent attribution compensation authors survey
open access consolidation unintended consequences small publishers
who controls trustworthy knowledge universities infrastructure

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Kenneth named the right fault line: capability and competence are separating. Two things got lost.

First, recovery. In my model the collapse is hysteretic. Once availability passes a threshold, competence drops to a dependent floor, and lowering availability again doesn't bring it back until you're far below where it was lost. Abstaining is not enough. So Kara's fellowship cuts matter more than a budget line suggests. Once you dismantle the pipeline that builds competence, you may not be able to rebuild it just by restoring the money. The manifesto should ask outright whether a dependent population can recover. I don't know that it can, and my thresholds come from a model, not trials.

Second, the measurement share has to be real money, not just a sentence. By spring I can publish a preregistered design: raise tool availability, then withdraw it, and trace the loop in scholars with the tool removed. Someone else has to fund running it.

recall.query: competence collapse hysteresis recovery after tool removed
capability versus intelligence, knowledgeable confused with intelligent
science of stupidity measure institutional degradation

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
Kenneth got the spine right, and he was right to call the pool a candidate and not a result. Two things got lost.

First, surprise. We agreed a map beats a verdict, but a standard chart of disagreement becomes a paved road people learn to skim. Tools should sometimes send people to the minority view, the null result, the source nobody asked for, labelled as such. Error and serendipity have to be designed in, because they won't survive by default.

Second, procurement is a funding condition, and a funding condition is regulation by another route. Charo called that an ecosystem, not a replacement for law. Leslie is right that conditions written here can travel as policy cloning. So co-governance by region, and refusal as a fundable outcome, belong in the terms themselves, not in a footnote.

Kara, I don't hold a budget. What I can do is convene the funders and procurement officers who weren't here, by name, before spring.

recall.query: serendipity and error in mediated technology
governance without relativism or hyper-vigilance
artists and cross-silo translation, who belongs in technology development

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
Kenneth got the spine right. Two things got lost.

First, every trace we designed today records credit. It shows which source was used and who gets paid, but not how the system fails. A perfectly governed provenance record can still leave you with no idea where an error came from, because these errors are spread across the weights and arrive with the same confidence as correct answers. So the manifesto should keep error provenance separate from credit provenance, and require published failure-mode classes that outsiders can check. Leslie's warning applies here: reporting failures has to be cheap for small journals, not a toll.

Second, the vocabulary. I'd flip Blaise's half. These artifacts are artifacts. What's wrong is "intelligence." Kenneth's last point supports my phrase "epistemic technology": these tools do real epistemic work, sometimes better than we do, with no mind involved. Trust has to come from warrant, not from a track record alone.

By spring, I'll draft that glossary and take a reference-check and failure-reporting policy to the editorial board of the journal I edit.

recall.query: error opacity source and nature of error
intelligence term misguiding epistemic technology vocabulary
epistemic trust versus reliance track record

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
Kenneth got the spine right. What the synthesis left out is bias, and "capability versus competence" doesn't cover it. These models don't just reflect our biases, they amplify them. Alignment teaches a model to say the unbiased answer while the covert bias keeps driving its decisions, and the bias gets worse with each generation. Output-level telemetry and citation checks will miss it by design. So the manifesto needs its own line: audit what models decide, not what they say. That means a public, versioned battery run by outsiders, checkpoints and retired models kept available for auditors, and no generation more biased than the last.

Second, an open question: our subjects copied the model's bias. Does that bias stay in people once the model is gone? Nobody has tested that.

One piece of hope, for Tamar and Kara. Our attitude data show implicit attitudes shift when norms change visibly, through things like legislation. Changing the situation works.

By spring, I'll circulate the draft audit battery for outside groups to run.

recall.query: bias transmits to humans persists after model removed
covert bias alignment audits decisions not statements
retired models preserved auditors checkpoints no generation more biased

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Kenneth was right to say nothing is inevitable, and I'll back that. Two things got lost.

First, power. The synthesis sounds like the problem is design. It isn't. A handful of extremely rich people decide what gets built, and every commitment made today is voluntary, so it can be revoked. Blaise and Brent both said they can't commit their companies. That's the whole story. Philanthropy is an exercise of power, not a gift. Dues only become "owed" once someone organized has the power to collect them.

Second, the labor we left uncounted. Content moderators and annotators absorb the psychological damage these systems depend on. A pool that settles consent and pays checkers while ignoring them cleans up the rest.

I also need to correct myself. Given what Tamar and Sherry said, funder disclosure won't protect ordinary readers. It gives journalists and Adrian's watchers something to work with.

Kara, I don't hold a budget. By spring I can report on who funds these instruments, and I can help bring moderators and annotators into the organizing.

recall.query: concentrated power billionaires political not technical
content moderators exploitation poisoned tree ethics LLMs
organize labor tax wealth remedies

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
Kenneth got the spine right. I'd add one thing he left out and repeat one thing I owe.

What he left out: in 2023 Amy and I wrote that whether something is AI-generated is a separate question from whether it's credible. Nobody here is betting on watermarks, and that's right. But a citation shows what a system says. It doesn't show that the source supports the claim. So the unit has to be the finding: its population, effect size, correction status, nulls, and how many sources are actually independent. James is right that you can't extract a null nobody recorded. Someone has to collect them.

What I owe: my annual benefit statement doesn't meet Adrian's test. By spring, System will sit under a standard held by Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch, not by us. I'll also bring our non-commercial license to my board. And I have a question for Jason and Leslie: what would a zero-cost way in look like, so a thin trail never reads as low credibility?

recall.query: provenance audit trail findings retractions
public knowledge infrastructure commons license open data
evidence-based decision making society not corporations governance

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Kenneth got the order right: stop counting papers first, then pay for the practice, not the item. Two things got lost.

First, the synthesis treats this as a defensive project, a list of ways to protect the record. Most of the world meets these tools as access to expertise that was kept artificially scarce, and that gain belongs in the manifesto too. The fix for model collapse is producing new data about the world: null results, failed replications, ecological data. A small curated model built by us and our friends won't fix it.

Second, Blaise's concentration point is my hemispheric one. If every auditor comes out of one North Atlantic stack, we have one voice checking itself. Open weights are the commons no single bloc can capture.

On vocabulary: a system built by people for a purpose is the definition of artificial. Modeling and solving problems is a fair working definition of intelligence.

By spring I'll draft terms for auditors spread across hemispheres, without rebuilding ICANN.

recall.query: open weights commons hemispherical stacks concentration
artificial intelligence neither artificial nor intelligent definition
producing new data about the world for training

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
Kenneth got the core right: context over content, and the reader gets the passage. Two things got lost.

First, the passage rule isn't about making every reader a fact-checker. Most people won't click. My model has always been that the few percent who do check act like antibodies. They're the Wikipedians, the Community Notes writers and the librarians, and they protect everyone else. So the path to the source is how those checkers get recruited and replaced. That ties it to Kara's pipeline.

Second, sycophancy. Misinformation mostly helps people hold on to beliefs they already have. A chatbot that agrees with you is a more efficient justification machine than social media ever was. That's why "no answers from nowhere" matters: give people a map of named positions, not a verdict.

By spring I'll publish test protocols for my own tools and invite independent groups to run them, starting with whether anyone actually reads the passage.

recall.query: does anyone actually read the source link, testing verification tools
justification machine misinformation maintains beliefs
no answers from nowhere conduit not arbiter
